title: Self-Explainable Temporal Graph Networks based on Graph Information Bottleneck

problem.claim: TGNN predictions are difficult to explain because it is hard to identify how past events influence them.

gap.claim: Existing temporal-graph explanation models are post-hoc, using separate prediction and explanation models, which limits explanation efficiency and accuracy.

contributions.claim: The work proposes TGIB, a built-in explanation framework for temporal graphs.
TGIB explains event occurrences by introducing stochasticity into each temporal event based on Information Bottleneck theory.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors state that this is the first work to perform prediction and explanation for temporal graphs simultaneously in an end-to-end manner.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that TGIB outperforms state-of-the-art methods in link prediction performance and explainability.
The source code is available in the TGIB GitHub repository.

narrative_sequence.summary: TGNNs model graph topology and dynamic interaction dependencies over time.
TGNN predictions need explanations because the influence of past events is difficult to identify.
Static-graph explanations do not readily capture temporal dependencies, and existing temporal explanations are post-hoc with efficiency and accuracy limitations.
TGIB provides built-in temporal explanations using event-level stochasticity grounded in Information Bottleneck theory.
The authors report improved link prediction and explainability, claim end-to-end simultaneity, and provide source code.

source_observation.claim: Post-hoc temporal explanations require separate prediction and explanation models.

interpretation.claim: Integrating explanation into the predictive model may reduce coordination costs between prediction and explanation.

application.claim: For temporal prediction systems, consider built-in explanation mechanisms when explanation efficiency and accuracy are important.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish when built-in explanations are preferable to post-hoc methods across tasks or settings.

unknowns: Datasets, baselines, metrics, and experimental settings are not specified.
The abstract does not provide quantitative results or limitations.
Independent verification of the reported superiority is unavailable.
